terms.short: A long, broad rise in prices
terms.definition: A long period in which prices rise broadly and investors are confident. A common rule of thumb is a rise of 20% or more from a recent low.
examples: We've been in a bull market since the 2020 low, with only short breaks.
terms.fill: Nifty has climbed steadily for two years and most stocks are up: a ____.
wrong: A market where only large companies trade
A single day of strong gains
A market run by big institutions

terms.short: A long, deep fall in prices
terms.definition: A long period of falling prices and gloomy sentiment. A common rule of thumb is a fall of 20% or more from a recent peak.
examples: Small caps are in a bear market, down 25% from the peak, even though Nifty is holding up.
terms.fill: An index that has fallen 22% from its peak over six months is in a ____.
wrong: A market where most traders are short
A single bad day on the exchange
A market closed for a holiday

calcs.q: An index falls from 30,000 to 24,000. How big is the fall, and what does the rule of thumb call it?
calcs.why: (30,000 − 24,000) ÷ 30,000 = 20%, the usual line for a bear market.

terms.short: A strong rise in prices
terms.definition: A period of strong, sustained buying that pushes prices up, over days or weeks. Rallies can happen inside a bull or a bear market.
examples: Banks led the rally after the RBI cut rates.
terms.fill: After the rate cut, buyers rushed in and Nifty jumped 4% in three days: a sharp ____.
wrong: A protest outside the stock exchange
A slow drift lower in prices
A meeting of shareholders

terms.short: A sharp wave of selling
terms.definition: A quick, heavy bout of selling that pushes prices down, often set off by bad news or fear.
examples: The IT sell-off came after a US client cut its tech budget.
terms.fill: Bad news hit and investors dumped shares all afternoon: a broad ____.
wrong: An offer for sale by promoters
A company selling one of its businesses
Selling at the end of the financial year

terms.short: A fall of about 10% from a peak
terms.definition: A fall of roughly 10% to 20% from a recent peak, often seen as a pause in a longer rise rather than a turn into a bear market.
examples: After a 10% correction, valuations look reasonable again.
terms.fill: Nifty is 12% off its high, more than a dip but not a bear market: a ____.
wrong: A fix to a mistake in a company's accounts
A cancelled trade
A change to an index's members

calcs.q: Nifty peaked at 26,000 and now stands at 23,400. How far has it fallen?

terms.short: A sudden, very steep fall
terms.definition: A sudden, very steep fall in prices over a day or a few days, usually driven by panic. Unlike a correction, it happens fast.
examples: The March 2020 crash took Nifty down nearly 40% in weeks.
terms.fill: The market fell 13% in a single day: that's a ____, not a slow decline.
wrong: A fall in trading volumes
A failure of the trading app
A slow decline over a year

terms.short: The highest price ever reached
terms.definition: The highest level a stock or index has ever traded at. Above it there's no one sitting on old losses waiting to sell.
examples: Nifty is at an all-time high, and FPIs are still buying.
terms.fill: When an index trades above every price in its history, it's at an ____.
wrong: The highest price of the day
The price at the IPO
The upper circuit for the day

calcs.q: The previous record was 25,000. The index is now at 25,500. How far above the old high is it?

terms.short: Highest price in the past year
terms.definition: The highest price of the last 52 weeks. Its twin, the 52-week low, is the lowest. Both are shown on every quote screen and used as a quick sense of where a stock sits.
examples: It's 30% below its 52-week high; is it cheap or broken?
terms.fill: The highest price a stock has traded at over the last year is its ____.
wrong: The highest price in a single week
The yearly high of the whole index
The analyst's target for next year

calcs.q: A stock trades at 450. Its 52-week high is 600. How far below the high is it?

terms.short: Price level where falls tend to stop
terms.definition: A price level where buyers have stepped in before and stopped falls. Traders watch it closely, and a break below it is seen as a bad sign.
examples: 24,000 is strong support for Nifty; it bounced there twice.
terms.fill: The stock has bounced off ₹800 three times, so traders see ₹800 as ____.
wrong: A price fixed by the exchange
A broker's helpdesk
Buying by the company's promoters

terms.short: Price level where rises tend to stall
terms.definition: A price level where sellers have shown up before and capped rises. Once the price breaks above it, old resistance often turns into support.
examples: It keeps failing at 1,500; that's resistance until it closes above it.
terms.fill: The stock has turned down from ₹1,500 four times, so ₹1,500 is ____.
wrong: A cap set by the exchange
Opposition from shareholders
Selling by the company's founders

terms.short: Price pushing through a key level
terms.definition: When a price moves decisively above resistance, or below support, usually on heavy volume, which traders take as the start of a new move. A move down through support is often called a breakdown.
examples: Clean breakout above 1,500 on twice the usual volume.
terms.fill: After months stuck under ₹1,500, the stock closed at ₹1,560 on heavy volume: a ____.
wrong: A stock leaving an index
A sudden stop in trading
A company splitting into two

terms.short: Investors happy to take risk
terms.definition: A mood in which investors favour riskier assets, such as shares, small caps and emerging markets, because they're confident about growth.
examples: Risk-on today: small caps up 2%, gold and bonds lower.
terms.fill: Small caps are flying and gold is falling; the market is in ____ mode.
wrong: A rule that allows more leverage
A switch that turns on trading
Buying only insured investments

terms.short: Investors cutting risk and seeking safety
terms.definition: A mood in which investors pull back from riskier assets and move to safer ones, such as government bonds, gold or cash, usually because of fear.
examples: Risk-off after the war headlines: gold up, small caps down 3%.
terms.fill: War news hits, shares fall and gold jumps: a ____ day.
wrong: Switching off a trading algorithm
A market holiday
Selling only at a loss

terms.short: Selling to lock in gains after a rise
terms.definition: Selling after a rise to lock in gains, which can pull prices back even when there's no bad news. Indian market reports often blame a dip on it.
examples: Nifty slipped on profit booking after five days of gains.
terms.fill: After a 15% run in a month, investors sold to lock in gains: that's ____.
wrong: Recording profits in the company's books
A broker's fee on profitable trades
Tax paid on short-term gains

terms.short: Selling in fear, at almost any price
terms.definition: Heavy selling driven by fear rather than analysis, where investors dump holdings at almost any price to get out.
examples: Margin calls set off panic selling in the small caps.
terms.fill: Investors dumped shares at any price as the market plunged: ____.
wrong: Selling a stock you don't own
Selling according to a set plan
Selling by company insiders

terms.short: Final wave of selling as holders give up
terms.definition: The last, heavy wave of selling when even patient holders give up. Volume spikes and prices plunge, and it often comes close to a bottom.
examples: That volume spike looked like capitulation; the selling has dried up since.
terms.fill: After weeks of falls, a final day of huge-volume selling as holders throw in the towel is ____.
wrong: A company admitting to fraud
Promoters selling their whole stake
A broker shutting down

terms.short: Buying for fear of missing out
terms.definition: Fear of missing out: buying because prices are rising and others seem to be making money, rather than because of a careful view on value.
examples: Retail FOMO is back: every IPO is oversubscribed 100 times.
terms.fill: You buy a stock after a 50% jump only because your friends made money on it: that's ____.
wrong: A rule that limits buying
A type of futures order
Fear of selling too early

terms.short: Buying after a fall, expecting a recovery
terms.definition: Buying after a price falls, on the view that the longer rise will resume. It works in bull markets and can hurt badly in bear markets.
examples: Every 3% fall gets bought; buy-the-dip is the only trade that's worked this year.
terms.fill: Nifty fell 3% and you added more, expecting the uptrend to resume: you ____.
wrong: Buy only at the day's lowest price
Buy a stock just before its dividend
Buy shares in a cheap IPO

terms.short: Brief rebound in a steep fall
terms.definition: A short, weak recovery during a steep fall, after which the decline carries on. It's only clear in hindsight.
examples: Up 8% today, but I think it's a dead cat bounce; nothing has changed.
terms.fill: The stock fell 40%, bounced 10% in two days, then fell to new lows: a ____.
wrong: A stock delisted from the exchange
A recovery to an all-time high
A rebound that ends a bear market

calcs.q: A stock falls from 500 to 300, then bounces to 330. How big is the bounce?
calcs.why: (330 − 300) ÷ 300 = 10%, and it has only won back 30 of the 200 lost.

terms.short: Rising price forces shorts to buy back
terms.definition: A sharp rise that forces short sellers to buy back to limit losses, and their buying pushes the price up even faster. In India it shows up mostly in futures, where traders hold shorts overnight.
examples: Huge short build-up in the futures, then good results: classic short squeeze.
terms.fill: Heavy shorting, then surprise good news, and shorts rushing to buy back: a ____.
wrong: A cut in the margin allowed for shorts
A ban on short selling
A fall that rewards short sellers

terms.short: A position too many investors share
terms.definition: A position held by so many investors that, if the story changes, everyone tries to exit at once and the price moves violently.
examples: Long private banks is the most crowded trade among FPIs right now.
terms.fill: Every fund is long the same defence stocks, so any bad news could cause a rush for the exit: it's a ____.
wrong: A stock with very high trading volume
A trade split among many brokers
An IPO with many applicants

terms.short: Rushing into safe assets in a scare
terms.definition: When investors rush out of risky assets into safe ones, such as government bonds, gold or cash, during a crisis or scare.
examples: Flight to safety: the 10-year bond yield fell 15 bps as shares tanked.
terms.fill: When a crisis hits and money pours into government bonds and gold, it's a ____.
wrong: Moving money out of India
Buying airline shares
Closing all positions before a holiday

tf.s: In a flight to safety, government bond prices usually rise.
tf.why: Investors buy bonds, which pushes their prices up and yields down.

terms.short: Stuck between a steady high and low
terms.definition: When a price moves back and forth between a fairly steady high and low for a while, with no clear trend.
examples: Nifty's been range-bound between 24,000 and 25,000 for two months.
terms.fill: The stock has traded between ₹480 and ₹520 for three months: it's ____.
wrong: Limited by a circuit band
Allowed to trade only in lots
Held within a fund's limits

terms.short: A sideways pause after a big move
terms.definition: A pause after a strong move in which the price trades sideways in a tightening range, as the market digests the move.
examples: Healthy consolidation after a 30% rally; I'd wait for the breakout.
terms.fill: After a 40% rise, the stock has moved sideways in a narrow band for weeks: ____.
wrong: Two companies merging
A fund merging two schemes
Reducing the number of stocks you hold

terms.short: Prices moving steadily one way
terms.definition: A market moving steadily in one direction, with higher highs and higher lows in an uptrend, or the reverse in a downtrend.
examples: In a trending market, buying breakouts works; in a range, it gets you chopped up.
terms.fill: Each rise beats the last high and each dip stops above the last low: a ____.
wrong: A market where one stock is popular on social media
A market with record trading volumes
A market that follows the US

terms.short: Sharp move one way, then a sharp reversal
terms.definition: When the price jumps one way and then quickly reverses, catching traders on both sides and triggering their stop-losses.
examples: Got whipsawed: stopped out on the drop, then it ripped back up.
terms.fill: Bought the breakout, got stopped out on the drop, then watched it soar: a classic ____.
wrong: A cut in brokerage fees
A trade done on two exchanges
A steady fall in prices

terms.short: Opening well above the last close
terms.definition: When a stock or index opens well above the previous day's close, leaving a gap on the chart, usually after overnight news.
examples: Gap-up opening on the results; let's see if it holds.
terms.fill: It closed at ₹1,000 and opened at ₹1,050 after strong results: a ____.
wrong: A rise in the spread between bid and ask
A rise that fills an earlier fall
A jump in trading volume

calcs.q: A stock closed at 1,000 and opens at 1,040. How big is the gap?

terms.short: Opening well below the last close
terms.definition: When a stock or index opens well below the previous day's close, leaving a gap on the chart. A stop-loss can't protect you from it.
examples: Gap-down on the fraud news; stops filled 8% below their levels.
terms.fill: Bad news overnight, and the stock opened 7% below yesterday's close: a ____.
wrong: A fall in the bid-ask spread
A drop in volume
A stock leaving an index

tf.s: A stop-loss order always protects you from a gap-down.
tf.why: If the price opens below your stop, you exit at that lower price.

terms.short: Risen so far, so fast, a pullback looks likely
terms.definition: When a price has risen so far, so fast, that traders expect a pause or pullback. Many use the RSI momentum indicator, where a reading above 70 counts as overbought.
examples: RSI at 82; it's overbought, so I'd wait for a dip.
terms.fill: After nine straight up days and an RSI of 80, traders call the stock ____.
wrong: Sold to too many buyers in an IPO
Held by too many funds
Bought on too much margin

terms.short: Fallen so far, so fast, a bounce looks likely
terms.definition: When a price has fallen so far, so fast, that traders expect a bounce. On the RSI indicator, a reading below 30 counts as oversold.
examples: Oversold, but oversold can stay oversold in a bear market.
terms.fill: After a 25% drop in two weeks and an RSI of 22, the stock looks ____.
wrong: Short sold by too many traders
Sold below the IPO price
Sold by promoters

tf.s: An oversold stock must bounce soon.
tf.why: It only suggests a bounce is more likely. In a bear market, stocks can stay oversold for a long time.

terms.short: Sharp fall, then an equally sharp rebound
terms.definition: A sharp fall followed by an equally quick recovery, so the chart looks like a V. Indian shares did this in 2020, regaining their pre-Covid level within months.
examples: Nobody expected a V-shaped recovery after March 2020.
terms.fill: The index crashed 35% in a month and was back at its high six months later: a ____.
wrong: A slow recovery over many years
A recovery led by one stock
A rebound that fails

calcs.q: An index falls 40%. How much must it then rise to get back to where it started?
calcs.why: From 100 to 60 is −40%. Getting from 60 back to 100 needs a 40 ÷ 60 ≈ 67% rise.

terms.short: Huge fall and rebound within minutes
terms.definition: An extremely fast, deep fall that reverses within minutes, usually caused by an erroneous order or algorithms reacting to each other. On 5 October 2012, a mistaken order sent Nifty down about 15% in minutes.
examples: The 2012 flash crash was one fat-finger order hitting every bid.
terms.fill: Nifty fell 15% and recovered within minutes after an erroneous order: a ____.
wrong: A crash in the exchange's computer systems
A slow fall over a week
A fall in the price of flash memory makers

terms.short: How many stocks join a move
terms.definition: How many stocks are taking part in a market move. Good breadth means most stocks are rising with the index; poor breadth means a few big names are carrying it.
examples: Nifty is up, but breadth is awful: two stocks fell for every one that rose.
terms.fill: The index rose, but only five heavyweights went up while most stocks fell: poor ____.
wrong: The number of stocks listed on an exchange
The range between a day's high and low
The total market value of all listed companies

terms.short: Rising stocks divided by falling stocks
terms.definition: The number of stocks that rose in a session divided by the number that fell. Above 1 means more rose than fell.
examples: A/D ratio of 0.4 on NSE today; the index hides how bad it was.
terms.fill: 1,800 stocks up and 1,200 down gives an ____ of 1.5.
wrong: The ratio of buy orders to sell orders
Rising volume divided by falling volume
New highs divided by new lows

calcs.q: On NSE, 1,800 stocks rose and 1,200 fell today. What's the advance-decline ratio?
calcs.why: 1,800 ÷ 1,200 = 1.5, so three stocks rose for every two that fell.

terms.short: A rise in which most stocks take part
terms.definition: A rally in which most stocks and sectors rise, not just a few large ones. Traders see it as healthier than a narrow rally.
examples: Finally a broad-based rally: mid caps and small caps up more than Nifty.
terms.fill: Banks, IT, pharma, mid caps and small caps all rose together: a ____.
wrong: A rally in only the largest stocks
A rally spread over many weeks
A rally led by foreign investors

terms.short: Money moving from one sector to another
terms.definition: Investors moving money from one sector to another, for example out of IT and into banks, as views on growth, rates or valuations change.
examples: Rotation out of FMCG into capital goods has been the trade this quarter.
terms.fill: Funds are selling pharma and buying autos as the economy picks up: ____.
wrong: Changing the companies in an index
A fund manager moving between fund houses
Moving shares between demat accounts

terms.short: Stocks that hold up when the economy slows
terms.definition: Stocks whose earnings stay steady whatever the economy does, such as FMCG, pharma and utilities. Investors hide in them during downturns.
examples: In a slowdown, money hides in defensives like HUL and Sun Pharma.
terms.fill: With a recession feared, funds buy FMCG and pharma, the classic ____.
wrong: Shares of defence manufacturers
Stocks protected by a stop-loss
Stocks with high debt

tf.s: Defence manufacturers are always defensive stocks.
tf.why: Defensive means steady earnings in a slowdown, not the defence industry.

terms.short: Stocks that rise and fall with the economy
terms.definition: Stocks whose earnings swing with the economic cycle, such as autos, metals, cement and capital goods. They tend to do well in recoveries and badly in slowdowns.
examples: Cyclicals are leading; the market is betting on a capex upturn.
terms.fill: Metals and autos jump as the economy recovers, true to form as ____.
wrong: Stocks that pay dividends every year
Stocks that trade in the same daily pattern
Stocks that rejoin an index every year

terms.short: Stocks that swing more than the market
terms.definition: Stocks that typically move more than the market in both directions, such as small caps, metals and PSU stocks. They lead rallies and get hit hardest in sell-offs.
examples: In risk-off, high-beta names get dumped first.
terms.fill: When Nifty rises 1%, these stocks often rise 2%, and fall 2% when it falls: ____.
wrong: Stocks being tested before listing
Stocks with the most analysts
Stocks with high dividend yields

terms.short: How much risk investors want to take
terms.definition: How willing investors are to take risk at a given time. Strong risk appetite shows up as money going into small caps, IPOs and leveraged trades.
examples: Risk appetite is strong: SME IPOs are oversubscribed 300 times.
terms.fill: When IPOs are flooded with bids and small caps soar, ____ is high.
wrong: The maximum loss SEBI allows a trader
A fund's required return
The margin a broker asks for

terms.short: Money moving into or out of markets
terms.definition: Money moving into or out of a market, sector or fund type. In India, FPI and DII buying and selling figures come out every evening and are closely watched.
examples: FPIs were net sellers of ₹4,000 crore today, but DIIs bought it all.
terms.fill: Every evening, traders check FPI and DII ____ to see who bought and sold.
wrong: Interest earned by funds
Cash a company receives from sales
Fees fund houses charge

terms.short: Prices far above any sensible value
terms.definition: When prices rise far above any reasonable value, driven by speculation and the belief that they'll keep rising. Bubbles usually end in a sharp fall.
examples: SME IPOs listing at 90% premiums look like a bubble.
terms.fill: Prices tripled in a year on hype alone, with no earnings to back them: a ____.
wrong: A small company with few shares
A pause after a rally
A stock trading in a narrow range

terms.short: A sudden, steep rise driven by FOMO
terms.definition: A sharp, fast rise driven more by fear of missing out than by fundamentals, often late in a bull market. It can be followed by a sharp fall.
examples: This isn't earnings, it's a melt-up; everyone's chasing.
terms.fill: Late in a bull run, the index shoots up 15% in a month with no change in earnings: a ____.
wrong: A slow fall in prices
A rally that melts away in a day
A rise in metal prices

terms.short: A rare shock nobody saw coming
terms.definition: A rare, unexpected event with a huge impact that seems obvious only afterwards. The term was popularised by Nassim Taleb.
examples: Covid was the black swan nobody's risk model had.
terms.fill: A sudden, unforeseen event that crashes markets worldwide is a ____.
wrong: A stock that rises against the market
A rare stock with no debt
A short seller who predicts a crash

terms.short: Trouble spreading from one market to others
terms.definition: When trouble in one company, sector or country spreads to others, as investors sell anything that looks similar or has links to it.
examples: The IL&FS default in 2018 caused contagion across NBFCs.
terms.fill: One lender defaults, and shares of every similar lender crash: that's ____.
wrong: A virus that shuts down trading
Copying another fund's portfolio
A stock rising with its sector

terms.short: Risk from a known upcoming event
terms.definition: The risk of a big price move around a known event, such as an election result, an RBI policy decision, the Union Budget or a company's results.
examples: We're cutting positions ahead of the budget; too much event risk.
terms.fill: Traders cut positions before the election results because of the ____.
wrong: The risk that a trade fails to settle
The risk of an exchange outage
The risk in a company's events business

terms.short: Risk that sudden news moves prices
terms.definition: The risk that a sudden news headline, such as a tariff threat, a raid or a policy rumour, moves prices sharply without warning.
examples: Tariff talk is pure headline risk; one tweet and the IT stocks swing 3%.
terms.fill: A single surprise news report can knock the stock 5%: it carries high ____.
wrong: Risk of being in the news for fraud
The risk in media company shares
The risk of misreading a chart's title

terms.short: Weeks when most companies report results
terms.definition: The few weeks after each quarter when most companies report results. In India, listed companies must report within 45 days of a quarter's end, or 60 days for the full-year results.
examples: Earnings season kicks off with TCS next week.
terms.fill: Mid-January to mid-February, when most companies report December-quarter results, is ____.
wrong: The time of year when dividends are paid
The financial year's last quarter
The months before the Union Budget
terms.note: These deadlines come from SEBI's listing rules (LODR).

terms.short: Cash and credit suddenly dry up
terms.definition: When cash and credit suddenly become scarce, so borrowers can't roll over loans and sellers can't find buyers without big price cuts. India's NBFCs went through one after IL&FS defaulted in 2018.
examples: The liquidity crunch forced NBFCs to sell good assets at a loss.
terms.fill: Lenders stop lending and even good bonds can't be sold: a ____.
wrong: Too many shares trading at once
A cut in a company's dividends
A drop in an exchange's trading volume on a holiday

terms.short: Cutting risk by shrinking positions
terms.definition: Reducing risk by cutting positions, leverage or exposure to volatile areas, often ahead of uncertainty or after losses.
examples: Funds are de-risking into the election; cash levels are up.
terms.fill: Ahead of the results, the fund sold small caps and raised cash: ____.
wrong: Buying insurance for a building
Removing a stock from surveillance
A regulator lowering margin rates
